1.title: Containers and Containerization
1.text: Welcome to Module 1: Containers and Containerization. This module is in the Kubernetes Fundamentals domain, and it covers the topic called Containerization. By the end you will be able to do four things. Explain why containers are used and how they differ from virtual machines. Describe images, layers, registries, tags and digests. State what the O C I standards and the container runtime stack do. And choose the right image pull policy.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Packs the Storefront
1.text: At Harbor Books, the developer has the storefront as code, plus a list of the libraries it needs. The team wants it to run the same way on a laptop, in testing and in the cluster. Today the shop is deployed by copying files to servers, and every server is slightly different. That is the problem containers solve. In this module the storefront becomes a container image.

1.title: Why Containers: Portable, Dense, Consistent
1.text: A container packages an app with the files it needs, so it behaves the same wherever it runs. Containers decouple the app from the host infrastructure. Compare that with a virtual machine. A virtual machine is a whole operating system with its own kernel. A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel, so more apps fit on less infrastructure. The diagram shows two virtual machines, each with a guest operating system, next to three containers on one shared kernel. Exam tip: a container is an isolated process, not a small virtual machine.

1.title: From Image to Running Container
1.text: A container image is a ready-to-run package: the code, the runtime it needs and its libraries. A container is a running instance of an image, and one image can start many containers. The life cycle has three steps: build, ship, run. You build the image from a Docker file, push it to a registry, then a node pulls it and runs it. Images are immutable, which means a change produces a new image. Exam tip: the image is the template, and the container is what runs.

1.title: Image Layers
1.text: An image is built from layers. Each layer is a set of file system changes. You start from a base image and add layers for libraries and your own code. Because images are immutable, a change adds a layer on top instead of editing what is below. And when a node pulls an image, it downloads only the layers it does not already have. Exam tip: layers make images efficient, because shared layers are stored and pulled once.

1.title: Registries, Tags and Digests
1.text: An image name has up to four parts. The registry says where the image is stored. If you leave it out, Kubernetes assumes the Docker public registry. Then comes the name of the image itself. Then an optional tag, a label for a version. A tag can be moved to a different image, and no tag means the tag latest. Last, an optional digest, a hash of the image content, which never changes. To run exactly the same image everywhere, reference it by digest. Exam tip: tags move, digests do not.

1.title: Image Pull Policy
1.text: The image pull policy decides when the kube let pulls an image. If Not Present pulls only when the image is not already on the node. Always asks the runtime to pull every time a container starts, and layers that are already cached are reused. Never does not pull at all, and the container fails to start if the image is missing. When you leave the policy out, Kubernetes chooses. The tag latest, or no tag, gives Always. A version tag or a digest gives If Not Present. Exam tip: latest or no tag means Always, and a version tag means If Not Present.

1.title: OCI: The Open Standards
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic, so it comes from the older curriculum and is kept at recognition level. The Open Container Initiative, O C I, develops open standards for containers. The image specification defines the format of an image. The runtime specification defines how to run a container from an unpacked file system bundle. The distribution specification defines the A P I protocol for distributing content through registries. And run C runs containers according to the O C I specification. Exam tip: O C I means image, runtime and distribution.

1.title: What a Container Is Made Of: Namespaces and cgroups
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum, because it explains what a container is under the hood. A container is a process on the host's kernel, isolated and limited by Linux features. Namespaces give a process its own isolated view of a system resource. Control groups, called C groups, put processes in groups whose resource use can be limited and monitored. The kube let and the runtime use C groups to enforce C P U and memory requests and limits. Exam tip: namespaces isolate and C groups limit, and a Linux namespace is not a Kubernetes namespace.

1.title: The Runtime Stack: CRI, containerd, CRI-O, runc
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum and old wording. The kube let talks to a container runtime through the Container Runtime Interface, the C R I. Container D and C R I O are runtimes that implement the C R I. A low-level runtime such as run C creates the container. The old built-in bridge to Docker Engine was called docker shim, and it was removed in version one point twenty-four. Images built with Docker still run on any runtime. Exam tip: Kubernetes needs a C R I runtime such as container D or C R I O, and docker shim is gone.

1.title: Dockerfile and Multi-Stage Builds
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. A Docker file is a text file of instructions for building an image. A multi-stage build uses several From lines, and each one starts a new stage. In the snippet, the first stage builds the storefront. The second stage starts from a small base image and copies only the finished program from the first, with copy dash dash from. Everything you do not copy is left behind, so the final image is smaller. Exam tip: multi-stage builds keep build tools out of the final image.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Containers
2.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Container or V M: containers share the host's kernel, and a virtual machine brings its own. Image or container: the image is the template, and the container is a running instance. Tag or digest: tags can move, and a digest never changes. Pull policy: latest or no tag means Always, and a version tag means If Not Present. Docker or C R I: Kubernetes needs a C R I runtime, and docker shim was removed in version one point twenty-four. And O C I: image, runtime and distribution. Exam tip: decide first which layer a question is about.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. Containers are isolated processes that share the host kernel, so they are lighter than virtual machines. Images are immutable stacks of layers, and the container is the running instance. An image name has a registry, a name, and a tag or a digest, and the pull policy follows the tag. The standards are the O C I image, runtime and distribution specifications, and the runtime chain is kube let, C R I, container D or C R I O, then run C. Builds use a Docker file, and multi-stage builds give smaller images. Now seven practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which statement correctly compares containers with virtual machines? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Containers are isolated processes that share the host's kernel, which is why more of them fit on the same infrastructure. A virtual machine carries a whole operating system with its own kernel. Containers do not need a hypervisor, and they are isolated from each other.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The Harbor Books team tests an image and then wants production to run exactly the same image. How should the Pod refer to it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A digest is a hash of the image content, so it identifies one exact image. Tags, including latest, can be moved to point to a different image, and a registry can hold many versions under one name.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A container uses the image storefront colon one point four, and the Pod does not set an image pull policy. Which policy does Kubernetes apply? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. When the policy is left out, a version tag gives If Not Present, and so does a digest. Only latest, or no tag at all, gives Always. Never is used only when it is set explicitly.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. The Harbor Books team pushes a rebuilt storefront image as storefront colon one point five. A node already runs storefront colon one point four, and only the top layer differs. What does the node download? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Images are stacks of layers, and the runtime downloads only the layers that are not already cached. Tag one point five is a different reference from one point four, so a pull is needed, but the shared layers are reused.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Which O C I specification defines how images are pushed to and pulled from a registry? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The distribution specification defines the A P I protocol for distributing content. The image specification defines the image format, the runtime specification defines how a bundle is run, and the Pod specification belongs to Kubernetes, not to the O C I.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. What is the Container Runtime Interface, the C R I? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The C R I is how the kube let talks to a runtime such as container D or C R I O. The image format and the registry protocol are O C I specifications, and grouping processes to limit resources describes C groups.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A team reads that docker shim was removed in version one point twenty-four. What does that mean for its cluster? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Kubernetes needs a C R I compatible runtime on each node. Images built with Docker still run on any runtime, the direct Docker Engine integration is gone rather than switched off, and no hypervisor is needed for containers.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, B: containers share the host's kernel. Question two, D: a digest identifies one exact image. Question three, A: a version tag gives If Not Present. Question four, C: only missing layers are downloaded. Question five, D: the distribution specification covers registries. Question six, A: the C R I connects the kube let and the runtime. Question seven, C: nodes need a C R I compatible runtime.
